# Quick Take: AMD’s Helios as a Plug-and-Play AI Appliance Standard

AMD’s Helios rack scale compute appliance combines AMD’s CPU, GPU, and Ethernet hardware portfolio with the ROCm software framework to provide an integrated, turn-key solution. Notably, Helios uses OCP’s Open Rack Wide (ORW) form factor, which is 1.2 m wide and 1.3 m deep, providing 44 OU (Open Unit) of rack space in a standard cabinet—an OU measures 48mm tall, rather than the traditional 44.45mm of a typical 19” server rack. Power is delivered through the back of the tray over a 50 V DC power bus, with connections for the liquid cooling system provided through blind-mate, quick disconnect plugs. AMD configures the Helios appliance with two groups of nine compute trays (each measuring 1 OU) with six switch trays (also measuring 1 OU) in the middle, with management/power at top, and power at the bottom.

Each compute tray four integrates AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs and one AMD EPYC 9006-series SP7 server CPU (a 96-core EPYC 9G76 in the standard configuration), paired with 16 DIMM sockets each populated with a 64 GB DDR5 ECC RDIMM, and five slots for E1.S SSDs connected to the CPU. Each networking board includes four or six AMD Pensando (“Vulcano”) NICs for the scale-out / back-end network, with each tray incorporating two networking boards. Additionally, each tray incorporates a PCIe slot for a Pensando (“Salina”) DPU for the front-end network, and a separate system management module with an Ethernet interface for a total of 72 GPUs in one rack. Assuming the MI455X’s undisclosed TDP is the same or higher than the prior generation, 72 GPUs represent more than 100,000 watts in a single rack. Each switch tray integrates two Ethernet switches, and each of the 12 switches is connected directly to all 72 GPUs. GPU-to-Switch communication is conducted over copper cable cartridges at the rear of the rack.

In the broader context of the AMD Helios appliance, the combined CPU, GPU, and networking technologies combined with the ROCm software are a considerably more integrated product than AMD’s prior offerings, and one that stands shoulder-to-shoulder with NVIDIA’s rack-scale compute appliances. That said, NVIDIA retains its reputation as being market-leading but at a significant price premium. NVIDIA’s CUDA framework is not necessarily a “moat” keeping customers from switching, as the friction for porting software from CUDA to ROCm is substantially easier than it was a year ago, aided—slightly ironically—in part by AI-assisted software porting. AMD’s answer is an improvement in integration: Helios retains the familiarity of x86-64 (while NVIDIA is pushing its Vera Arm CPU), not that AI workloads are particularly ISA-dependent, and ROCm continues to receive significant development and investment.

That said, hyperscale cloud providers are generally (but not exclusively) reliant on NVIDIA GPUs and are investing heavily in semi-customized AI ASICs (e.g., AWS Trainium, Google TPU) to serve internal and customer workloads, but those ASICs are captive silicon. Today, Google Cloud and Amazon Web Services offer no AMD Instinct-equipped instances, though Microsoft Azure does (despite the development of Maia AI ASICs). OpenAI and Anthropic are pursuing task-optimized silicon in partnership with Broadcom, though this is as much a result of financial engineering as it is one of semiconductor engineering. At this juncture, custom silicon could become stifling in implementation as models, architectures, and available production time at leading-edge semiconductor fabs change.

Smaller cloud providers such as Oracle and neoclouds such as CoreWeave ostensibly benefit from the ready-to-serve integration that Helios provides; this would be the most obvious route to market for AMD and its OEM partners. While there are enterprise customers for AI infrastructure, to the extent that enterprises are adopting AI, it is typically as cloud-delivered SaaS or IaaS—considering the power delivery and space requirements of deploying leading-edge AI infrastructure. Which, notably, neither AMD nor NVIDIA meaningfully disclose the TDPs of next-generation GPUs, making analysis on that basis something of a stab in the dark, particularly absent non-vendor-provided software benchmarks.
